query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a two‐step heat treatment consisting of a high-temperature solutionizing step followed by an aging step to trigger the precipitation of fine, coherent Ti2Ni-type intermetallic particles in a titanium–nickel primary high-entropy alloy will enhance its elevated-temperature mechanical properties relative to the same alloy without this treatment.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast or homogenized single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloy containing approximately 40 at% titanium, 40 at% nickel, and ~20 at% of additional refractory/supporting elements (e.g., V, Cr, or Al) that meets the HEA compositional criteria.
generation.intervention: A two-step heat treatment: first, solutionize the alloy at approximately 1100°C for 1 hour in an inert atmosphere to homogenize and dissolve any preexisting precipitates; second, age the alloy at approximately 600°C for 1–2 hours to induce controlled precipitation of fine Ti2Ni-type intermetallic particles.
generation.conditions: Conduct the solution treatment at ~1100°C for 1 hour followed by a controlled aging treatment at ~600°C for 1–2 hours in an inert (oxygen‐free) atmosphere to minimize oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Uniformly distributed, nanoscale, coherent Ti2Ni-type precipitates embedded in the single-phase solid-solution matrix.
generation.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening, whereby the fine, coherent intermetallic precipitates hinder dislocation motion at elevated temperatures, thereby enhancing yield strength and creep resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the non-heat-treated baseline alloy, the heat-treated alloy will exhibit higher elevated-temperature yield strength and improved creep performance due to the precipitation strengthening effect.
generation.baseline: The as-cast or homogenized alloy without the two-step heat treatment, characterized by a single-phase solid-solution microstructure lacking fine precipitates.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to HEAs with a primary composition of approximately 40 at% Ti, 40 at% Ni, and ~20 at% additional refractory/supporting elements (e.g., V, Cr, Al) within the standard HEA compositional limits (5–35 at% each element) and evaluated for performance at temperatures up to ~700°C.
generation.uncertainty: The exact precipitate size, volume fraction, and distribution may vary depending on the precise aging duration and temperature; there is also some uncertainty regarding the potential for over-aging or precipitate coarsening at prolonged exposure, which could diminish the strengthening effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy using identical casting and homogenization procedures. Subject one set to the two-step heat treatment (solutionizing at 1100°C for 1 hour and aging at 600°C for 1–2 hours under inert atmosphere) and retain the other set as the non-heat-treated baseline. Characterize both sets using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to assess the presence, size, and uniformity of precipitates, and perform elevated-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., yield strength and creep tests at ~700°C).
measurements: TEM imaging to determine the size, density, and coherence of precipitated Ti2Ni-type particles
X-ray diffraction to confirm phase constituents and detect any secondary phase formation
Mechanical testing (tensile or creep tests) at elevated temperatures to quantify yield strength improvements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance compared to the baseline samples, OR if the TEM and XRD analyses do not confirm the formation of uniformly dispersed, nanoscale, coherent Ti2Ni-type precipitates, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) contain more than five alloying elements in a composition range of 5–35% and with slight atomic size variation. Recent narrative studies on HEA thin films and their synthesis through deposition techniques such as sputtering have highlighted the need for determining the corrosion behaviors of such alloys used as biomaterials, for example, in implants. Coatings composed of biocompatible elements such as titanium, cobalt, chrome, nickel, and molybdenum at the nominal composition of Co30Cr20Ni20Mo20Ti10 were synthesized by means of high-vacuum radiofrequency magnetron (HVRF) sputtering. In scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis, the coating samples deposited with higher ion densities were thicker than those deposited with lower ion densities (thin films). The X-ray diffraction (XRD) results of the thin films heat treated at higher temperatures, i.e., 600 and 800 °C, revealed a low degree of crystallinity. In thicker coatings and samples without heat treatment, the XRD peaks were amorphous. Precipitation hardening is a common method to enhance the mechanical properties of Ti alloys, HEAs, and MEAs [,,]. Via control of the precipitation treatment, it is possible to regulate the size and distribution of the precipitated phases, allowing for adjustments in various alloy properties. Precipitation hardening treatment can be divided into single-step (direct heat treatment) and two-step (solution treatment + heat treatment) processes. Two-step precipitation hardening treatment can produce a finer and more uniformly distributed α phase in β-Ti alloys than the single-step process, which can significantly increase the yield strength, ductility, and corrosion resistance of Ti alloys []. Moreover, the fine and uniformly distributed α phase does not significantly increase the elastic moduli of Ti alloys []. Furthermore, the precipitated phases can fill surface defects, improving the corrosion resistance of Ti alloys [,]. A significant amount of research has been conducted on the precipitation hardening of high-entropy alloys [,,,,]. proposals.material_system: Equiatomic high-entropy alloy with titanium and nickel as primary constituents (e.g., ~40 at% Ti, ~40 at% Ni, plus ~20 at% distributed among refractory/supporting elements such as V, Cr, or Al to fulfill the HEA definition)
proposals.intervention: Apply a two‐step heat treatment (solutionizing followed by aging) designed to precipitate fine, coherent intermetallic particles (for example, a Ti₂Ni-type phase) within the matrix.
proposals.conditions: First, solution treat at ≈1100°C for 1 hour in an inert atmosphere to homogenize; then, age at ≈600°C for 1–2 hours to trigger controlled precipitation.
proposals.structural_mediator: Nanoscale, coherent intermetallic precipitates uniformly dispersed in the single-phase solid-solution matrix.
proposals.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening, where the fine precipitates hinder dislocation motion at elevated temperatures, thereby increasing yield strength and creep resistance.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared with the as-cast (or non-heat-treated) baseline, the alloy will exhibit enhanced high-temperature strength and improved creep performance, with finer precipitate size and uniform dispersion offering a superior resistance to deformation.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By using heat treatment to induce a precipitation-strengthened microstructure in a Ti–Ni–primary HEA, the intervention specifically targets the elevated-temperature mechanical shortcomings while leveraging the unique compositional balance of Ti and Ni.

proposals.material_system: Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy modified with a minor addition of a refractory element (e.g., Ti35Ni35Mo15V15, with Mo selected for its high melting point and impact on mixing enthalpy)
proposals.intervention: Incorporate a controlled small fraction (≈10–15 at%) of Mo to the alloy formulation to promote the formation of a dispersed intermetallic phase (such as a Mo-bearing Laves phase) during solidification and subsequent heat treatment.
proposals.conditions: Melt-cast alloy under argon with the designated composition, followed by a post-casting anneal at ≈900°C for 2 hours to allow the nucleation of the Mo-induced intermetallic particles.
proposals.structural_mediator: A dual-phase microstructure consisting of a dominant single-phase Ti–Ni matrix interspersed with finely dispersed, thermally stable Mo-rich intermetallic precipitates.
proposals.mechanism: The intermetallic particles act as obstacles to dislocation motion and help stabilize the microstructure at high temperatures, reducing grain growth and enhancing creep resistance.
proposals.predicted_outcome: The alloy will show higher yield strength and improved elevated-temperature mechanical stability relative to an otherwise equivalent Ti–Ni primary HEA without Mo, as evidenced by refined intermetallic dispersion and slower coarsening kinetics.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This strategy explores the under-investigated regime of Ti and Ni as primary constituents by modifying the alloy chemistry with a refractory addition, thereby directly addressing the need to improve high-temperature performance through microstructural engineering.

proposals.material_system: Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy (e.g., near-equiatomic Ti–Ni supplemented with minor amounts of elements such as Al and V for entropy stabilization)
proposals.intervention: Subject the cast alloy to severe thermomechanical processing—specifically, hot rolling followed by rapid annealing—to induce ultrafine-grained (UFG) microstructure and abundant high-angle grain boundaries.
proposals.conditions: Hot rolling performed at ≈900°C with a reduction of 50–70%, followed by rapid annealing at ≈850°C for 30–60 seconds to recrystallize while retaining UFG structure; processing under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation.
proposals.structural_mediator: An ultrafine-grained microstructure featuring a high density of grain boundaries that act as barriers to dislocation motion.
proposals.mechanism: Grain-boundary strengthening (Hall–Petch effect) coupled with thermally stable subgrain structures enhances high-temperature mechanical properties by inhibiting dislocation glide and grain coarsening.
proposals.predicted_outcome: The processed alloy is expected to display superior yield strength and creep resistance at elevated temperatures compared to the baseline cast alloy, as verified by a significant refinement in grain size and uniform substructure.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This intervention leverages thermomechanical processing—a different structural lever—to improve high-temperature capability in a Ti–Ni based HEA, complementing compositional approaches with deformation-induced microstructural stability.

proposals.material_system: Bulk Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy (designed within the compositional bounds with ~40 at% Ti, ~40 at% Ni, and minor additions of elements such as Cr or V for entropy stabilization)
proposals.intervention: Apply a high-temperature resistant surface coating via high-vacuum magnetron sputtering of a related Ti–Ni HEA coating, followed by a post-deposition annealing step to promote inter-diffusion and formation of a protective transition layer.
proposals.conditions: Deposit a coating of approximately 100–150 μm thickness using optimized ion densities (e.g., 20–30 µAcm⁻²) at low substrate temperatures, then anneal at ≈800°C for 30–60 minutes in a controlled atmosphere to avoid oxidation and ensure strong chemical bonding.
proposals.structural_mediator: A graded interface featuring a transition layer (potentially a TiNi intermetallic or solid solution) that bonds the coating to the substrate, with the coating itself exhibiting a refined microstructure.
proposals.mechanism: The coating not only serves to protect the substrate against high-temperature oxidation but also introduces beneficial residual compressive stresses and a refined microstructure on the surface, thereby enhancing load-bearing capacity and delaying creep deformation.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to uncoated samples, the coated alloy should demonstrate improved elevated-temperature performance, with reduced oxidation rates, enhanced surface strength, and better overall mechanical stability in long-term high-temperature tests.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By focusing on surface modification—a distinct lever in materials engineering—this hypothesis directly targets the degradation mechanisms at elevated temperatures, offering a supplemental route to enhance mechanical properties in Ti–Ni primary HEAs.

critiques.addresses_problem: The intervention focuses on mitigating surface degradation (oxidation and creep) by applying a protective coating, which can improve high‐temperature performance, but it only indirectly addresses bulk mechanical properties.
critiques.constraints: It respects the material system and operating conditions by using a Ti–Ni based HEA coating; however, the introduction of a coating might lead to compositional or thermal expansion mismatches with the substrate.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically sound: a high-temperature resistant coating can reduce oxidation, introduce beneficial residual stresses, and refine surface microstructure.
critiques.feasibility: The use of high-vacuum magnetron sputtering and subsequent annealing are well-established, though controlling inter-diffusion and adhesion is challenging.
critiques.evidence: The proposed method is supported by deposition and post-treatment protocols in PMC10054136 where sputtering and heat treatment are used, although for thin films.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is poor adhesion or interfacial delamination during thermal cycling, potentially undermining the mechanical stability at high temperatures.
critiques.fix: Optimize the graded interface and inter-diffusion parameters to ensure robust adhesion and minimize thermal expansion mismatch between the coating and substrate.

critiques.addresses_problem: The strategy directly targets high-temperature limitations by modifying the alloy’s chemistry to form finely dispersed intermetallic precipitates that hinder dislocation motion and stabilize the microstructure.
critiques.constraints: The composition (Ti35Ni35Mo15V15) remains within the definition of a HEA with titanium and nickel as primary elements, though the 15 at% Mo must be carefully controlled.
critiques.physical_soundness: The formation of Mo-induced intermetallic (e.g., Laves phase) is a plausible mechanism for precipitation strengthening at elevated temperatures.
critiques.feasibility: Melt-casting followed by annealing to nucleate precipitates is an established method in alloy design.
critiques.evidence: Precedents for using refractory additions to induce precipitate strengthening in high entropy alloys are found in PMC8074761 and PMC9571103, which discuss sigma and related phases enhancing yield strength.
critiques.main_risk: The risk is that the precipitates may grow too coarse during annealing, potentially embrittling the alloy rather than strengthening it.
critiques.fix: Refine the heat-treatment schedule (temperature/time) to ensure the formation of a fine, homogeneously dispersed precipitate rather than coarse particles.

critiques.addresses_problem: This intervention targets the problem by using a two‐step heat treatment to induce precipitation strengthening, thereby improving yield strength and creep resistance at high temperatures.
critiques.constraints: The treatment is applied to an equiatomic Ti–Ni primary HEA with additional elements to satisfy the HEA criteria, so it stays within the stated compositional boundaries.
critiques.physical_soundness: Precipitation of fine, coherent Ti2Ni-type intermetallic particles is a well-understood mechanism for strengthening and enhancing high-temperature properties.
critiques.feasibility: The two-step heat treatment (solutionizing then aging) is a standard technique in alloy processing and is feasible with current methods.
critiques.evidence: Supporting evidence comes from studies (e.g., PMC10744552 and PMC8074761) that confirm precipitation hardening in similar systems enhances mechanical performance.
critiques.main_risk: There is a risk of over-aging or precipitate coarsening at the elevated temperatures, which would reduce the strengthening effect.
critiques.fix: Optimize aging time and temperature to control precipitate size and maintain a fine, coherent distribution under service conditions.

critiques.addresses_problem: This approach aims to enhance elevated-temperature mechanical properties by generating an ultrafine-grained structure; however, grain refinement alone may not fully address high-temperature instabilities.
critiques.constraints: The intervention applies to a Ti–Ni primary HEA with minor stabilizing additions and fits within the compositional and processing constraints, yet ultrafine grains are prone to coarsening at high temperatures.
critiques.physical_soundness: While the Hall–Petch effect from an ultrafine-grained structure is physically valid, its effectiveness at elevated temperatures is limited by the tendency for rapid grain growth.
critiques.feasibility: Severe thermomechanical processing via hot rolling followed by rapid annealing is feasible; similar protocols are documented in PMC9506522.
critiques.evidence: Evidence from studies like PMC9506522 shows that thermomechanical processing can refine grain structures; however, long-term stability at high temperatures remains a concern.
critiques.main_risk: The principal risk is that the ultrafine-grained microstructure will undergo rapid grain coarsening during prolonged high-temperature exposure, negating the benefits achieved.
critiques.fix: Incorporate additional grain boundary pinning strategies, such as minor alloying with particles or precipitates, to stabilize the ultrafine-grained structure under high-temperature conditions.
